english.html: Especially in criminal matters, in which proof by oath is not lawful,

In criminal causes, because the proofs must be certain, indubitable, and clearer than the day, the tendering of the oath is not received <sup class="mk" data-key="a">a</sup>; considering especially that if it had place in these matters, it would easily come about that crimes and calumnies, by the collusion of the parties, would be covered over and remain unpunished <sup class="mk" data-key="b">b</sup>.

notes.citation: Code 4.19 (De probationibus), the last law, l. Sciant cuncti (C. 4.19.25, Constantine)
notes.gloss: Accusers must bring a matter to public cognisance fortified by fit witnesses, or by the plainest documents, or by indications ad probationem indubitatis et luce clarioribus — "indubitable for proof and clearer than daylight"; Coras's "clearer than the day" is this phrase.

notes.citation: Decretals X 5.22 (De collusione detegenda), c. 1 and the whole title
notes.original: c j. & tout le titre, de col luſ. detegend
notes.gloss: The title on detecting collusion between the parties to a suit, where the accused and accuser agree to a feigned contest; its first chapter annuls a sentence obtained by such collusion.

english.html: Added to which, there are persons who are so superstitious that they would not dare to swear, even were it for things evidently true.

Ulpian in a certain place, speaking of a legacy made by a testator on condition that the legatee should swear, says that such a condition must be rejected, and that the legatee may boldly demand the legacy without taking the oath with which the testator charged him: so that, says he, he may neither lose the legacy by being unwilling to swear, nor win it by perjuring himself. For there are some, says the Jurisconsult, too ready to swear, in contempt of religion; others fearful of the divine power even to superstition, so that even of things which they know and are well assured of, they nevertheless would not, nor would dare to, swear <sup class="mk" data-key="a2">a2</sup>.

notes.citation: Digest 28.7 (De condicionibus institutionum), l. Quae sub condicione (D. 28.7.8 pr.–§ 1, Ulpian)
notes.original: l. quæ ſub conditione. D de cond. inſt
notes.gloss: Quae sub condicione iurisiurandi relinquuntur, a praetore reprobantur: dispositions left under condition of an oath are disallowed by the praetor, who provides that the beneficiary shall neither lose the inheritance or legacy by omitting the condition nor be compelled to swear shamefully; for some are too ready to swear in contempt of religion, others too timid through fear of the godhead, even to superstition — Coras's whole annotation is a paraphrase of this law.
